telescopes.name: James Webb Space Telescope

size.note: Primary mirror diameter, 6.5 m approximately (segmented beryllium).

telescopes.why: The largest and most powerful observatory ever sent to space.
results: Sees back over 13.5 billion years to the first galaxies born after the Big Bang
Mid-infrared views of dust and carbon-based molecules in star-forming nebulae

telescopes.name: Hubble Space Telescope

size.note: Primary mirror, 'nearly 8 foot (2.4 meter)'.

telescopes.why: The first large telescope in space for visible and ultraviolet light, and the first designed to be serviced by astronauts in orbit.
results: Discovery of dark energy
First precision measurement of the expansion rate of the universe
First exoplanet atmosphere detected and its elements determined

telescopes.name: Chandra X-ray Observatory

size.note: Outer diameter of the High Resolution Mirror Assembly (4 nested pairs of grazing-incidence mirrors).

telescopes.why: NASA's flagship X-ray mission and third Great Observatory, with the largest, most precisely shaped X-ray mirrors ever built, giving images 25 times sharper than any earlier X-ray telescope.
results: Traced the separation of dark matter from normal matter in colliding galaxy clusters
Observed the region around the supermassive black hole at the centre of the Milky Way
Imaged the glowing remains of exploded stars and the dispersal of elements

telescopes.name: Planck

size.note: Primary reflector 1.9 x 1.5 m; ESA gives the effective aperture as 1.5 m.

telescopes.why: ESA calls it the most sophisticated 'time machine' ever launched; it produced the most precise image of the cosmic microwave background.
results: Most precise map of the cosmic microwave background
Age of the Universe: 13.8 billion years
Revised cosmic make-up: 4.9% normal matter, 26.8% dark matter

telescopes.name: Gaia

size.note: Two telescopes, each with a rectangular primary mirror of about 0.7 m2 collecting area; ESA gives no single diameter.

telescopes.why: It built the largest and most precise 3D map of the Milky Way, measuring nearly two billion objects.
results: Showed the Milky Way's thick disc began forming 13 billion years ago
Revealed that our Galaxy merged with another large galaxy about 10 billion years ago
Measured the acceleration of the Solar System

telescopes.name: Kepler

size.note: NASA: '3-foot (1-meter) diameter aperture telescope'; the primary mirror itself is 1.4 m (4 ft 7 in).

telescopes.why: NASA's first planet-hunting mission and the first to find Earth-size planets in the habitable zones of their stars.
results: More than 2,600 exoplanet discoveries
Showed the galaxy holds more planets than stars
First confirmed system with more than one planet transiting the same star (Kepler-9)

telescopes.name: Spitzer Space Telescope

size.note: 34-inch (85 cm) infrared telescope.

telescopes.why: The fourth and last of NASA's Great Observatories, and the first telescope to capture light directly from planets outside the solar system.
results: First direct capture of light from extrasolar planets (2005)
Revealed the TRAPPIST-1 system of seven Earth-size planets (2017)
Found a huge new ring of Saturn (the Phoebe ring)

telescopes.name: COBE

size.note: Three instruments (DIRBE, FIRAS, DMR), none with one headline aperture.

telescopes.why: It showed that the cosmic microwave background has a near-perfect blackbody spectrum and produced the first 'baby picture' of the universe, earning the 2006 Nobel Prize in physics.
results: CMB spectrum a nearly perfect blackbody at 2.725 K
First detection of intrinsic CMB anisotropy, at one part in 100,000
Detection of the cosmic infrared background

telescopes.name: Herschel Space Observatory

size.note: Primary mirror diameter, 3.5 m.

telescopes.why: The largest infrared space telescope launched before Webb, four times bigger than any earlier infrared space telescope.
results: Revealed networks of dust and gas filaments where stars form
Traced water from star-forming clouds to planet-forming discs
Found Comet Hartley-2's water has nearly the same isotopic ratios as Earth's oceans

telescopes.name: XMM-Newton

size.note: Diameter of the largest of 58 nested mirror shells in each of the three X-ray telescopes (700 mm). The Optical Monitor is a 30 cm telescope.

telescopes.why: The biggest science satellite ever built in Europe and, in ESA's words, the most powerful X-ray telescope ever placed in orbit.
results: Used X-ray echoes to map the surroundings of a black hole
First sighting of hot gas sloshing within a galaxy cluster
Found hot, diffuse gas helping close the gap in the cosmic budget of normal matter

telescopes.name: Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope

size.note: No mirror. Main instrument, the Large Area Telescope (LAT): peak effective area >8,000 cm2 (about 0.8 m2) at normal incidence. This is an area, not a diameter.

telescopes.why: It maps the gamma-ray sky from 8 keV to over 300 GeV, scanning the whole sky every three hours.
results: Discovered the Fermi Bubbles, structures spanning 50,000 light-years
First light seen from a gravitational-wave event (neutron-star merger)
More than 300 gamma-ray pulsars

telescopes.name: Compton Gamma Ray Observatory

size.note: Four instruments (BATSE, OSSE, COMPTEL, EGRET), none with one headline aperture.

telescopes.why: The second of NASA's Great Observatories and the first great gamma-ray observatory, covering six orders of magnitude in energy (30 keV-30 GeV).
results: Found that gamma-ray bursts are spread evenly across the sky
Discovered blazars as the main source of the highest-energy cosmic gamma rays
Mapped the Milky Way in the aluminium-26 gamma-ray line

telescopes.name: WMAP

size.note: Back-to-back primary reflectors of 1.4 x 1.6 m.

telescopes.why: It produced the first fine-resolution (0.2 degree) full-sky map of the microwave sky and put the 'precision' in precision cosmology.
results: Universe's age determined as 13.77 billion years, to within half a percent
Curvature of space within 0.4% of flat
Support for inflation from the pattern of density fluctuations

telescopes.name: TESS

size.note: Each of 4 identical wide-field cameras has a 10.5 cm entrance pupil; there is no single primary mirror.

telescopes.why: The first spaceborne all-sky transit survey for exoplanets.
results: More than 1,000 confirmed exoplanets
Nearly 6,000 confirmed or candidate exoplanets mapped by September 2025

telescopes.name: IRAS

size.note: Liquid-helium-cooled 0.6 m Ritchey-Chretien telescope.

telescopes.why: NASA's first infrared space telescope, which made the first all-sky infrared survey and doubled the number of known astronomical sources.
results: Discovered a disk of dust grains around the star Vega
Found six new comets
Revealed for the first time the core of the Milky Way

telescopes.name: Hipparcos

size.note: Primary mirror diameter, 290 mm (all-reflective Schmidt).

telescopes.why: The very first space mission for astrometry, measuring the positions of more than 100,000 stars 200 times more accurately than before.
results: Hipparcos Catalogue of 118,218 stars at the highest precision
Tycho Catalogue of 1,058,332 stars (Tycho-2: 2,539,913)

telescopes.name: Euclid

size.note: Primary mirror, 1.2 m.

telescopes.why: ESA's dark-Universe survey telescope; its NISP instrument has the largest field of view ever flown in space for an infrared instrument.
results: First major data release covering more than a billion objects
Discovered 31 of the most ancient quasars, including the two earliest known

telescopes.name: Swift

size.note: UV/Optical Telescope (UVOT) aperture, 30 cm. The gamma-ray Burst Alert Telescope is a coded-mask instrument with no mirror.

telescopes.why: A first-of-its-kind multiwavelength observatory built to catch gamma-ray bursts and slew to their afterglows within about 90 seconds.
results: First short gamma-ray burst with a detected afterglow (May 2005)
About 1,800 gamma-ray bursts and 1,400 supernovae observed by its 20th anniversary
All-sky high-energy X-ray survey

telescopes.name: NuSTAR

size.note: Derived: each of the two optics has a maximum radius of 191 mm (133 nested shells), so about 0.38 m across. Caltech does not state a diameter directly.

telescopes.why: The first telescope in orbit to focus high-energy X-rays (3-79 keV) into images.
results: First precise measurement of a black hole's spin
Contributed to the first-ever picture of a black hole

telescopes.name: Spektr-RG (eROSITA, ART-XC)

size.note: eROSITA: seven mirror modules of 54 nested shells each; ART-XC: seven modules. eROSITA has been in safe mode since 2022-02-26 (MPE), its survey paused; ART-XC works on.

telescopes.why: eROSITA made the first imaging all-sky survey in medium-energy X-rays (up to 10 keV); its first catalogue is the largest collection of X-ray sources ever published.
results: eRASS1 catalogue of about 900,000 X-ray sources, incl. ~710,000 active galactic nuclei and 12,000 galaxy clusters
More than 1,000 superclusters of galaxies identified
ART-XC all-sky survey (2021)

telescopes.name: Hale Telescope

size.note: 200-inch (5.1 m) Pyrex primary mirror

site.name: Palomar Observatory, Palomar Mountain, San Diego County, California, USA

telescopes.why: It was the largest effective telescope in the world from 1949 until 1993.
results: First official photographs taken by Edwin Hubble on 26 January 1949
Maarten Schmidt and collaborators identify the radio-loud objects 3C 273 and 3C 48 (quasars), 1963

telescopes.name: Hooker Telescope

size.note: 100-inch (2.54 m) mirror

site.name: Mount Wilson Observatory, San Gabriel Mountains, California, USA

telescopes.why: It was the largest telescope in the world from 1917 to 1949.
results: Hubble finds a Cepheid variable in the Andromeda Galaxy (1923), showing galaxies exist beyond the Milky Way
Hubble correlates galaxy distance with recession velocity, confirming the expanding Universe (1929)
First stellar diameter (Betelgeuse) measured by Pease and Michelson (1920)

telescopes.name: Arecibo Telescope
operators: Cornell University (1963-2011, for ARPA then NSF)
University of Central Florida (current manager for NSF)

size.note: 305 m (1,000 ft) fixed spherical reflector

telescopes.why: When inaugurated in 1963 it was the largest single-dish radio telescope in the world.
results: Demonstration of gravitational waves from a binary pulsar (Hulse and Taylor, Nobel 1993)
First discovery of extrasolar planets (around a pulsar, Wolszczan 1992-93)
Discovery of millisecond pulsars (Backer 1982)

telescopes.name: FAST
operators: National Astronomical Observatories, Chinese Academy of Sciences (NAOC)

size.note: 500 m active spherical reflector

site.name: Dawodang karst depression, Pingtang County, Guizhou Province, China

telescopes.why: It is by far the largest single-dish radio telescope in the world.
results: 224 pulsars discovered by 30 September 2020
Passed national evaluation and began formal operation on 11 January 2020

telescopes.name: Very Large Telescope

size.note: 4 × 8.2 m Unit Telescopes (Antu, Kueyen, Melipal, Yepun) + 4 movable 1.8 m Auxiliary Telescopes

site.name: Paranal Observatory, Cerro Paranal, Atacama Desert, Chile

telescopes.why: ESO's flagship, combining four 8.2 m telescopes into Europe's most productive ground-based observatory.
results: First image of an extrasolar planet
Tracking individual stars orbiting the supermassive black hole at the Milky Way's centre
Observation of the afterglow of the furthest known gamma-ray burst (at the time)

telescopes.name: Keck Observatory

size.note: 2 × 10 m primaries, each 36 hexagonal 1.8 m segments

telescopes.why: Their segmented 10 m mirrors made them the world's largest optical-infrared telescopes when built, and Keck II was the first large telescope to install adaptive optics (1999).
results: Confirmation of the accelerating expansion of the Universe
Discovery of a supermassive black hole at the centre of our Galaxy
Spectrum of the most distant galaxy ever recorded (at the time)

telescopes.name: ALMA
operators: in cooperation with the Republic of Chile

size.note: 66 antennas (54 × 12 m + 12 × 7 m) over baselines from 150 m up to 16 km

site.name: Chajnantor Plateau, Atacama Desert, Chile (about 5000 m)

telescopes.why: It is the most powerful millimetre/submillimetre telescope on Earth, giving images sharper than Hubble's at its wavelengths.
results: Image of the HL Tau protoplanetary disc that changed theories of planet formation
Einstein rings imaged in extraordinary detail
Detection of complex organic molecules in a distant protoplanetary disc

telescopes.name: Herschel's 40-foot telescope
operators: William Herschel (funded by King George III)

size.note: 48-inch (about 1.22 m) speculum-metal mirror in a 40 ft tube; size_m converted from 48 in

site.name: Observatory House, Slough (demolished): about the corner of Windsor Road and Herschel Street

telescopes.why: For about 50 years it was the largest telescope in the world.
results: Discovery of the sixth and seventh satellites of Saturn
Made the King's grant pay Caroline Herschel a salary as William's assistant, making her the first woman in England paid as an astronomer

telescopes.name: The Leviathan of Parsonstown

size.note: 72-inch (1.8 m) speculum-metal mirror in a 54 ft (16.5 m) wooden tube

site.name: Birr Castle Demesne, Birr (formerly Parsonstown), County Offaly, Ireland

telescopes.why: It was the world's largest-aperture telescope from 1845 until the Hooker telescope opened at Mount Wilson in 1917.
results: Discovered the spiral structure of galaxies, first recorded in the Whirlpool Galaxy (M51)
Spiral structure then identified in dozens of other 'spiral nebulae'

telescopes.name: Yerkes 40-inch refractor

size.note: 40-inch (about 1.02 m) objective lens; largest refracting telescope ever used

site.name: Yerkes Observatory, Williams Bay, Wisconsin, USA

telescopes.why: It is the largest refracting (lens) telescope ever used.
results: W. W. Morgan's 1951 discovery of the Milky Way's spiral-arm structure (Yerkes Observatory)
The 1897 dedication gathering formed the seed of the American Astronomical Society
Its photographic plate archive is used to study stellar motions and estimate dark matter in the Milky Way

telescopes.name: Lovell Telescope

size.note: 76 m (250 ft) fully steerable dish

telescopes.why: When completed in 1957 it was by far the world's largest steerable radio telescope; it is still the third-largest.
results: Tracked the rocket that launched Sputnik 1 within days of completion (October 1957)
Received the first photograph from the Moon's surface, from Luna 9 (February 1966)
Key role in pulsar research and tests of General Relativity

telescopes.name: Murriyang (Parkes)

size.note: 64 m dish

site.name: Parkes Observatory, near Parkes, New South Wales, Australia (Wiradjuri Country)

telescopes.why: It is one of the largest single-dish telescopes in the southern hemisphere dedicated to astronomy, and has found almost half of all known pulsars.
results: Prime receiving station for Apollo 11; received video of the first Moonwalk (July 1969)
Almost half of the more than 2000 known pulsars found with it

telescopes.name: Very Large Array

size.note: 27 active 25 m dishes (+1 spare) on a Y; A-configuration about 22.6 miles (36.4 km) across; arms 13 and 11 miles

site.name: Plains of San Agustin, near Socorro, New Mexico, USA

telescopes.why: One of the most productive radio telescopes ever built: 27 dishes on a Y, working as one telescope up to 36 km across.
results: Quickly confirmed the first gravitational lens, discovered optically in 1979
Revealed for the first time a 'mini-spiral' of hot gas at the Galactic Centre (1983)
Radar echoes indicating water ice in Mercury's polar craters (1991, 1994)

telescopes.name: Gran Telescopio Canarias
operators: GRANTECAN S.A. (Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias-led; Spanish State and Canary Islands government)

size.note: 10.4 m segmented primary (36 hexagonal segments, 75.7 m² collecting area)

site.name: Observatorio del Roque de los Muchachos, La Palma, Canary Islands, Spain

telescopes.why: It is the largest optical-infrared telescope in the world.
results: Key role (HiPERCAM) in discovering a ring around the dwarf planet Quaoar (2023)
Detection of a possible 'fossil fingerprint' of the Universe's first stars in galaxy NGC 1277 (2026)

telescopes.name: Subaru Telescope
operators: National Astronomical Observatory of Japan (NAOJ), NINS

size.note: 8.2 m effective-diameter single-piece primary mirror

site.name: Maunakea summit, Island of Hawaii, USA

telescopes.why: Its single 8.2 m mirror and wide-field cameras repeatedly set the record for the most distant known galaxy.
results: Broke the 'most distant galaxy' record multiple times; at one point 9 of the 10 most distant known galaxies were Subaru discoveries
Discovery of Himiko, a giant gas cloud about 12.9 billion light-years away
Hyper Suprime-Cam survey found about 200 protoclusters of galaxies about 12 billion light-years away

telescopes.name: Vera C. Rubin Observatory

size.note: 8.4 m Simonyi Survey Telescope with the 3200-megapixel LSST Camera, the largest digital camera ever built

telescopes.why: It carries the largest digital camera ever built and is running the 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time.
results: 2104 never-before-seen asteroids discovered in about 10 hours of First Look observations, including seven near-Earth asteroids
First Look images (23 June 2025) of the Trifid and Lagoon nebulae and the Virgo Cluster, showing about 10 million galaxies

telescopes.name: Extremely Large Telescope

size.note: 39 m segmented primary mirror

site.name: Cerro Armazones (3046 m), Atacama Desert, Chile

telescopes.why: When complete it will be the world's biggest eye on the sky.

telescopes.name: SKA-Low

size.note: 131,072 antennas in 512 stations, up to 74 km apart; 50–350 MHz

site.name: Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, Murchison, Western Australia

telescopes.why: Being built as one of the two SKA telescopes: the low-frequency array, in Western Australia.

telescopes.name: SKA-Mid

size.note: 197 dishes (SKA’s 15 m dishes with MeerKAT’s), up to 150 km apart; 350 MHz–15.4 GHz

telescopes.why: Being built as one of the two SKA telescopes: the mid-frequency array of dishes, in South Africa.
